newsitem.title: USA: Group proposes far-reaching changes for U.S. boardrooms.
newsitem.headline: Group proposes far-reaching changes for U.S. boardrooms.

text.p: A group that represents a cross-section of Corporate America's boards of directors Tuesday recommended far-reaching boardroom changes.

In a report by a blue-ribbon panel, the National Association of Corporate Directors stressed the need for boards to be independent of management and to achieve higher professional standards through periodic evaluations.
One of the panel's most critical recommendations was that boards limit the number of board seats any individual may hold, so a director may devote enough time to the boards he or she serves.

For example, the panel said that for chief executives and senior executives, companies should prefer individuals who hold no more than one or two public-company directorships, in addition to the executive's own board.

For other fully employed individuals, it said boards should pick those with no more than three or four public company directorships. For all others, it said boards should choose individuals who hold no more than five or six public company directorships.
The panel also recommended that boards:
* Limit the tenure of directors, to obtain fresh ideas and critical thinking from new board members;

* Designate a non-executive board chairman or other independent board leader to direct the most critical board functions, such as evaluating the performance of the CEO, the board itself and individual directors and ways to respond to crises;
* Establish an independent committee to oversee the board's governance responsibilities, including nominating new directors and setting/monitoring board performance goals;
* Operate independently of management and the corporation, avoiding or disclosing any business relationship that might be perceived as compromising independence.

Currently, there is no limit on the number of directorships an executive may hold. Also, while length of service on a board is deemed adding to a director's expertise on the corporation's business, critics contend that long tenures tend to create smugness and inflexibility.
Many of the panel members said they believe it is wise for corporations to have "not more than one or two" insiders on the board, and that boards should hire executive search firms to get new blood.

The NACD's recommendations are by no means binding. The Washington-based group represents about 1,800 top executives who serve on or deal with corporate boards. The companies in which they serve range from those belonging to the Fortune 500 or smaller, private and closely held firms.
"These recommendations are guidelines available that corporate boards may adopt, said NACD President John Nash.
While the NACD has made its sugggestions, he said, "It is my sense that instititutional shareholder groups should pressure boards to implement them."
If past recommendations regarding corporate governance are used as a gauge, Nash said he hoped that in the next three to five years, "our recommendations would be commonplace" in U.S. boardrooms.
"We need other people, not only CEOs, to be on boards of corporations," said Ira Millstein, the panel's chairman, who is senior partner at the law firm Weil, Gotshal & Manges LLP.
Millstein said naming more women and minorities to boards would be welcome. But choosing a director should be based on skills, not merely to "diversify" a board, he said.
"We are not creating a scorecard here," he said, urging corporations to consider what the panel believes to be the best industry practices.
The NACD had previously issued recommendations on changes in executive and director compensation and ways to evaluate CEOs.
